To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) lexical decision times are a function of the complexity of the verb's semantic event template, and (2) sentence processing times are a function only of the complexity of a verb's event template and not of the frequency with which the verb occurs in transitive and in-transitive constructions.

the processing of sentences is faster when the event template of the verb is simpler and that the complexity of the event template is not related to the probability with which the verb appears in transitive or intransitive sentences.

(i) the syntactic properties of verbs are encoded in the lexicons of the language users and that (ii) the syntactic information encoded in the lexica of the language users is encoded in the form of event templates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the representation and processing of verbs and the semantic and syntactic information associated with them.
a fundamental problem in cognitive linguistics: the nature of semantic representations of verbs and their role in sentence processing.
how the meaning of verbs is represented in the mind/brain and how this representation is used to process sentences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
event templates in verb lexicons are important for sentence processing, but not to the exclusion of other factors.
the syntactic information is encoded in the semantic event template of the verb, and that the event template of the main verb is the primary determinant of sentence complexity.

the syntactic structure of sentences is not encoded directly in the lexical representations for verbs, but rather that the syntactic information is encoded indirectly in the form of event templates that represent the semantic roles of participants in events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the syntactic structure of a sentence is not represented separately from the lexical information about the verbs that appear in the sentence.
syntactically-relevant information about the lexical representations of a verb is encoded in the event template.
the syntactic structure of sentences is not stored in the lexicon but is computed on the basis of the semantic event template encoded for each verb in the lexicon.
The main takeaway from our work is that
syntactically-relevant information about verbs is represented in the lexicon, and that the representation of this information in the lexicon affects sentence processing.
the syntactic information about verbs is stored in the lexicon and is not computed online.
the syntactic properties of verbs are encoded in the lexicons as semantic event templates.
